rules.reason: A dev.* fixture user with a committed password. Human users in production come from real sign-ups, never from the realm file.
A dev.* fixture user with a committed password. Alice and Bob share a tenant, which is what makes cross-tenant denial testable.
A dev.* fixture user with a committed password, in a second tenant.

The service account the API uses to give a self-registered account its own tenant. Development commits a fixed secret so a fresh checkout registers without configuration; a deployment takes it from KEYCLOAK_PROVISIONER_SECRET, which the preflight refuses to let stay a placeholder.
Self-registration needs verification mail to be of any use, so a deployment follows QUORUM_SMTP_ENABLED with it. Development always has mailpit and is always open.
Requiring a verified address without a relay would create accounts that can never be verified and therefore never sign in. It follows the same switch as registration for that reason.
The password-grant CLI client is a development convenience for fetching a token with one curl call. It must never exist in production.
Development reaches Keycloak over plain HTTP through Docker's port proxy, which Keycloak classifies as external. Production runs behind TLS and must enforce it.

Development delivers every mail to the mailpit container on a fixed internal address with no credentials. A deployment uses whatever relay the operator has, so host, port, TLS flags, sender addresses and the relay credentials all come from the environment at import time.

Password reset is only usable once mail can be delivered. Development always has mailpit, so it is on unconditionally. A deployment follows QUORUM_SMTP_ENABLED, so a stack without a relay never shows a 'Forgot password?' link that leads nowhere.
Development lists the local Vite, preview and compose origins. Production derives the single public origin from QUORUM_PUBLIC_URL at import time.
Same origins as redirectUris, as the CORS allow-list. Literal localhost in development, substituted in production.
The ## separated post-logout allow-list follows the same origins. Keycloak refuses a post-logout redirect the client has not declared, so this list drifting out of sync breaks sign-out.
